newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice files more charges in broker crackdown.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice files more charges in broker crackdown.

text.p: The Justice Department announced Thursday the second set of criminal charges against investment brokers accused of cheating their customers.

Attorney General Janet Reno told her weekly news conference that 17 brokers in 10 states have been charged or convicted for engaging in schemes involving elderly or unsuspecting investors. The brokers were targeted in a crackdown launched in late 1995.
"These investment advisers are accused of forging investor checks, making unauthorised transfers of client funds and using false or fictitious account statements," she said.

When the crackdown was unveiled in November 1995, charges were filed against 11 fired investment brokers in 10 different states. Most of the more recent cases also involved brokers who have been dismissed from their securities firms.
"Brokers may have gotten away with these crimes with little punishment before. Those days are over," Reno said, adding that more charges will be brought if necessary.

Among the 17 cases, William Russell, a former broker at Smith Barney, was charged in federal court in Tampa Wednesday with embezzling more than $200,000 from 12 clients. He has agreed to plead guity to fraud charges, the department said.

In Los Angeles, Henry Maxwell, a former broker at A.G Edwards & Sons Inc., was charged Tuesday with victimising an elderly client in a scheme in which he took about $280,000 worth of bonds, the department said.

The crackdown, which also involves the Securities and Exchange Commission, has targeted so-called "rogue brokers" who use various schemes, including forgery, unauthorised transfer of client funds and false account statements.
William McLucas, head of the SEC's enforcement division, said investors need to be wary about get-rich-quick schemes.

"Know your broker. Know who you're dealing with. Never buy something as a result of cold call, a high pressure sale. And when the pitch sounds like it's too good to be true, you ought to take that as an indication that it likely is," he said.
